I believe the motivation isn't only about saving money but to recycle, reuse, reduce, and to use more organic ingredients. it's called being penny wise and pound foolish. But whatever floats your boat, if saving is like a hobby for some people I can see them going nuts on certain things. I save to achieve goals, like traveling and early retirement, so for me I'm focused on different aspects of being frugal.

Yeah, at that point it's not about the pennies; rather it's become part of the person's value system and lifestyle. The sense of well being and satisfaction that comes from saving 50 cents on a bag of potatoes so overwhelms the awareness of having spent $5 on gas to drive across town that it's not even part of the savings equation any more. Basically it's no longer a rational decision but an emotional one. This is why accountants usually suck at running a business (I know they think otherwise but hey it's the truth); They are trained to look at numbers impartially and rationally, but business is not just about the numbers. Successful business people generally have an innate skill for balancing the emotional or gut side with the black and white or numbers side, which gives them the advantage over the rest of us.

For dried beans, there is NO comparison between canned and dried beans. One is a mushy, bland, covered in weird goop... the other can be cooked to the desired tenderness (I think mine with some firmness), you can impart Flavor to the things via the cooking water and know EXACTLY what you're putting in your mouth.

I make my own bread too, and pasta, english muffins, etc, etc, etc.... not for "frugal" sake (though it's FAR cheaper for me to make these items than to trade my time for money, then trade money for the pre-made item ~ given that I've been unable to obtain employment since 2009). I do this because I appreciate Quality, and knowing what I'm eating... plus, I, ya know, enjoy it.

I'm sure others feel the same with cleaners (we make our own granite cleaner, costs about 1/12th the price of commercially made stuff).

What about when someone spends hours upon hours of time on a ladder, scraping trim and then painting? Weeks of time to "save a few pennies"? Or "Sweat equity"?

I'd caution you to remember that not everyone has a steady supply of money, much less income to Replace that supply of money. For people like that, the cost savings between a 2lb bag of beans that'll make the equivalent of ~15 Cans of beans, for the cost of 2 cans of beans, adds up.

When you have more time than you have money, your time isn't quite as valuable.

I build little projects out of pallets I pick up from work. I even reuse some of the nails. It is a much longer and tougher process than if I would just start with a cheap sheet of plywood, but there are some bonuses. I am keeping a pallet out of the landfill. I am learning to best way to reuse what others see as waste. I enjoy figuring out way around the limitations of pallet wood. You may see it as a waste of time, I see it as time enjoying a hobby.

Sometimes being frugal is more about the learning process that will save you more in the long run than the pennies you save today.
